This is possibly the most complete use of Astrocade graphic resolution to date, and one of the largest most detailed play fields yet developed for Basic.  The amount of definition is fantastic.

I think the problem here is that Bally Alley is a database, but without the database.

I mean, there is a reason why people came up with dynamic webpages a decade ago or so.

With a db backend you can sort, filter, and search.  You can also build a web-based administration tool so you can add/edit/delete very easily.

If you're dealing with a small number of titles, like the cart titles for the Astrocade, a static site might make sense.  But the tape titles are clearly overwhelming to deal with.

As for putting stuff on a CD, I happen to think the era of multimedia CDs is kind of becoming passe' as always-on broadband connections become commonplace.  Information put on a CD is too easily obsoleted.  Most game databases are constant works in progress.  Look at AtariAge for instance.  Their game database for the 2600 is woefully lacking in the PAL department, and they've been working on their game database for several years now.  It really depends on the scope of the archival project.  Bally history has turned out to be much richer than anyone ever imagined.  New information just keeps crawling out of the woodwork.  Until you're really satisfied with the depth of the information you've gathered, I wouldn't even think about burning it to a CD.

The Game Player, #6  -- Vol. 5, pg. 82, March 14, 1983
-------------------

SECRET OF PELLUCITAR
L&M Software, Tape 15

    Here's another winner from L&M Software.  And guess what?  Along with fine game play, this game has excellent musical accompaniment by non other than George Moses.
    SECRET OF PELLUCITAR features the finest pre-game presentation this player has seen to date.  Before the actual game itself loads, a brilliant display of artwork, featuring the Starship Enterprise, flashing colors, oscillating sounds, and a neat musical selection are presented for your amazement.
    In this one or two player game, the television screen will display a large dome, filled with an intricate maze of tunnels that lead downward toward an innerdome, which contains a city of sky scrapers.  Your mission is to maneuver a blip through these tunnels, into the city and, finally, to a pedestal at the city's center.
    There is a choice of skill levels, from one to five.  The player starts with a score of 20,000 points, and looses points from that figure each time he runs into something.  In the two-player version, you will be treated to different sound effects and colors from the one-player version, and a different tune.  There are four different musical selections between the two versions.  In addition, you may select a difficulty level of one to nine, as you compete against the other player.
    In both versions, the player(s) must contend with the "Mysterious Force", a small square that moves somewhat randomly throughout the playfield, blocking tunnels and in some instances, creating momentary shortcuts.
    SECRET OF PELLUCITAR was described as enjoyable by all who played it.  The machine language programming and cartridge quality of this game make it worth its $15.95 price.  If there is any negative point concerning SECRET OF PELLUCITAR, it is only that it is somewhat difficult to see, due to the intricacy of the playfield which makes its details small.  This is not the kind of game you want to play on a 13 inch or smaller television screen.
    All things considered, this L&M game should prove enjoyable to most.  Although it is not the type of game that would be described as "exciting" or "action-packed", it is entertaining; and that's the bottom line to any game.

This week has been a busy one for me!  I've obtained a production model of the Bally Arcade from Toymax, the company that is FINALLY putting the Bally Arcade back into the hands of consumers.  By the end of May, if you live in the U.S., you should be able to get your hands on one of these little babies at plenty of places (including Walmart!).  Let me tell you, from my use of the production model, I think that all fans of the Bally Arcade will be pleased.  There are a couple of nitpicky things that I have about it, but Ill get to those later.

The name of this new little monster is Retro Astro.  Personally, I think that, while the name is clever, they could have gone with something else.  The name appeals to people who are already familiar with the Bally Arcade (aka Astrocade)-- and how many people is that?  Not more than a handful in terms of the potential buying crowd.  I havent actually seen a production box (or any box, for that matter), but, while I hate to admit it, I hope that it is colorful and aimed at small children.  It is the grandparents of these kids that are going to pick this videogame unit up for $19.95, site unseen (not having a clue about what they are buying for their grandkids birthday).  Without tapping this potential market, who would buy this?  The system IS about thirty years old.  Sure, there are the Atari versions of this little box (for instance, Atari Classics 10 In 1 TV Games-- also by Toymax), but these products are sold by name-brand loyalty and nostalgia-- both of which are in very short supply for this system.

Let me get to the function of this system.  First off, the system all fits in a joystick, but it looks NOTHING like the original Bally controller.  This one is obviously meant for smaller hands, and there is no trigger button.  Am I sad to see the gun-style joystick go?  Not at all!  While that controller had its pluses, it also got uncomfortable after you used it for a while.  This new joystick looks similar to the Atari 2600 controller, except that the joystick itself spins like a paddle.  Im not sure how they could have gotten away without the paddle feature, for it is used by the on-board menu and many games to select features (game number, lives, number of bullets, etc).  I was worried at first that the controller was going to take some getting used to, and it DID, but not nearly as long as I expected.  After a couple of hours I was using the controller like a pro.  My biggest problem with the controller is that since the whole joystick-top spins like a paddle sometimes that interferes with the normal left-right-up-down motion of the joystick, but with a little patience, youll get used to that too.

The Retro Astro plugs into your television using the standard audio-video cables that all the little hand-held units use nowadays.  So, say goodbye to all the RF Interference!  This opens up the possibility of getting decent screenshots of the included game using my computers videocard.

The BIGGEST problem that I have with the Retro Astro is that it runs on batteries.  Now, I know that quite a few of the handhelds DO run on batteries, but it would have been nice to have a way to at least also plug the unit into a wall wart or something, but no such feature exists.  On the plus side, the batteries do last for about eight hours.

There are twenty games included with the Retro Astro.  I can only guess that somehow Toymax now has the rights to these Bally games.  Youll find your old favorites here like Wizard of Wor (you have to play one-player, so that takes half the fun away).  Youll also find some real stinkers to, like Biorhythm (its not even Y2K compatible, come on!).  The complete list of games is:

1) Amazing Maze
2) Astro Battle (Yes, they STILL didnt use the Space Invaders name)
3) Bally Arcade Demo (again, neat, once or twice)
4) BASIC Demo (Not a game, but neat once or twice)
5) Baseball (Actually, the included paddle games are much better)
6) Biorhythm (even if it WAS Y2K compatible Why?)
7) Black Jack / Acey Deucy / Poker (Pretty fun!)
8) Brickyard / Clowns (Classic-- great use of the paddle controller)
9) Calculator (Um, its there in the ROM, but there is no keypad!)
10) Checkmate (Not the same without more than one player)
11) Cosmic Raider
12) Galactic Invasion (Another gem)
13) Grand Prix / Demolition Derby
14) Gun Fight (Built into ROM)
15) Pirates Chase
16) Red Baron / Panzer Attack
17) Scribbling
18) Space Fortress (Great game)
19) Treasure Cove
20) Wizard of Wor (Another classic, but only one player!?!)

If you check the list, youll notice that one game, Calculator isnt even usable-- but it DOES count toward the total of twenty games.  Another two games, BASIC Demo and The Bally Arcade Demo are also not a games, but they counts toward the overall total.  Also, the on-board ROM games count toward the twenty too (but, I guess thats okay as they ARE games).  Noticeably missing are Artillery Duel and Dog Patch, but they are both two-player only games.  There is one third party game included, and that is Treasure Trove, which is now in the public domain.

The way that you choose is a game is by picking it from a menu using the joystick and then pressing the fire button.  Once you do that, its like the system restarts by with the typical on-board menu that were all used to.  For instance, if you choose Space Fortress from the first menu, then you get the regular menu with Space Fortress as choice number one, which you then choose by turning the paddle (just as you would on the regular Bally Arcade).  If you choose any one of the four on-board ROM games, then you just see the menu as if no cartridge were plugged in at all.  This menu system is probably the best way that ToyMax could have gone.

The Astrocade really is emulated here (for the first time!) and after playing these games for most of the week to get a grip on this little item, I cant find anything wrong with the emulation.  So, as far as emulation goes, Toymax did a first rate job.  Now, let me get back to a few of the Nitpicky things that I talked about in the beginning of this article.  Now, for $19.99 I shouldnt expect everything, but here is a list of what is missing and I wish had been included:

1)  A little console like the Atari Flashback with a built-in keypad and Astro BASIC.
2)  A Cartridge slot (yea, I know, even the Flashback doesnt have that).
3)  A second controller so that two-player only games could be played.
4)  A selection of third-party games.

I know that the above list is asking a lot, but why not put it out there in case there is a Retro Astro 2?

So, in the end, this unit will allow us to play on a system that isnt going to overheat, and if nothing else, then THAT is great!

BTW: Ill be taking pictures of the unit and posting them in the next couple of days.

Astrovision/Astrocade:

Astrovision/Astrocade:
Sheet of paper to insulate board from bottom metal pan, that top plate is clipped to. There is at least 1 1/2" hole lining up with the vents in the bottom plastic casing.

Early Bally units:

The nine documents are:

1) jsa_backorders.pdf - 09/01/1975 - Backorder Policies and Procedures.

2) jsa_warranty_card.pdf - 1977 - JS&A National Sales Group Warranty Card.

3) jsa_oustanding_response.pdf - 11/07/1977 - Outstanding response and "How so cheap?"

4) jsa-bpa_delay.pdf December - 1977 - Initial production of Bally Professional Arcade delayed.

6) jsa_newspaper_question.pdf - 04/26/1978 - Newspaper answer, "Delay Blamed on Production."

7) jsa_tiny_basic_delay.pdf - 07/06/1978 - Tiny BASIC still on back order.

8) jsa_unable_to_fill_orders.pdf - 11/27/1979 - Response from liquidation sale so strong that not all
orders could be filled.

9) jsa-retraction_letter.pdf - 1979 - Retraction letter of advertisement in Wall Street Journal.

Reading these documents lets you know what it was like to be in the shoes of any of those poor folks that bought a Bally Professional arcade in 1977/78 and had to wait months for their machines, and then, once they got them, they had to wait months for Bally BASIC, and THEN, once they got THAT, their machines began to fail.  If you ever hear anyone ask WHY didn't the Astrocade do BETTER, then point them to these documents.  After reading these, perhaps you'll wonder how the Astrocade ended up getting a second chance with Astrovision at all...

Ballybin Bug Report
by Paul Thacker
April 29, 2006



Introduction

This report details some of the difficulties I've encountered when

using Ballybin and Astrowav.  I focus on the most recent iteration,

version 2 beta, but also reference version 1.4 and version 1.2 in

cases where these work better than the current version.  To ensure

consistency, I will include the versions I've used for testing, along

with .bat files I used to speed the processing.  For each version,

there is a batch-l1.bat file and a batch-l3.bat file.  Each calls

Ballybin to process every .wav file in the current directory, then

calls Astrowav to process every .bin/.bml file in the current

directory.  The only difference is that batch-l1.bat uses the -l1

option in Ballybin and batch-l3.bat uses the -l3 option.  Each file

referenced as an example is also included.

There are four major sections.  First, I discuss a problem converting

human-written .bml files to .wav files with Astrowav.  Next, I give

several examples of recordings that can't be processed with any

version of Ballybin.  It would be particularly good to get these

working, as there are no other known sources.  Next, I mention some

files that have been processed, but don't work correctly in the

current version.  These should be good for finding bugs, as the

recordings are proven to be good enough to make processing possible.

Finally, some desired additional features are mentioned.



Section 1:  BML conversion bug--

If you create a .bml file by hand and then run Astrowav v2 on it, the

resulting file can be very short and not allow the end of program

pointer to be set when loading.  In the example I created, if you run

the program, then list it, the comment on the first line is

overwritten.  See message #2536 in the Bally Alley group for more

details.  Example files:

weird_(hand_written)_[tim_hays].bml
weird_(no_end_of_program_pointer)_[tim_hays].wav



Section 2:  Recordings that won't process at all--

It seems that programs requiring a system with 16K or 32K RAM

expansion won't process correctly.  A large quantity of data is

processed, then the program crashes, regardless of what version is

used.  Examples:

pro_golf_(16K)_(raw)_[henry_sopko].wav
beatles_music_(minus_8_days_a_week)_(16K)_(raw)_[geroge_moses].wav
beatles_music_(32K)_(raw)_[geroge_moses].wav

Lance's recording of Sicko Therapy Session II won't process correctly

in any version of Ballybin I've tried.  Version 2 says it has a bad

stop bit.  Example:

sicko_therapy_session_ii_(raw)_[new_image].wav

RND Art I won't process correctly in any version of Ballybin.

Ballybin version 2 fails to halt.  This is particularly odd because

the raw recording will load perfectly.  Example:

rnd_art_i_(raw)_[new_image].wav

Mike White sent two versions of Lookout For The Bull.  The first one

won't process correctly.  Often there seems to be a problem in a

second, short load.  Ballybin version 2 fails to halt.  Example:

lookout_for_the_bull_(v1_from_mike_white)_(raw)_[wavemakers].wav

Some 2000 baud recordings from Russ Perry, Jr.'s tape collection won't

process correctly.  A recording Adam named written_for_brett won't

process at all in version 2 (with the -l3 option it fails to halt,

with -l1 it encounters a bad stop bit).  In other versions it will

apparently process, but the resulting program crashes when you load

it.  One of four early versions of ICBM Attack won't run after

processing in any version of Ballybin.  (The others work OK in at

least one version.)  Version 2 says it has a bad stop bit.  It's

possible this version simply isn't in a playable state.  Note that

ICBM Attack should be loaded with :RUN.

Examples:

written_for_brett_(raw).wav
icbm_attack_(v3)_(raw)_[brett_bilbrey].wav

A recording from Dave Ibach's tape collection looks like it should

have two loads, but only the first one will process in any version of

Ballybin.  I believe it is code intended to be loaded into the General

Video Assembler.  Such recordings have a fairly long load followed by

an extremely short load.  In this case, the second load on the tape is

very distorted and might not be recoverable.

Example:

all_machine_instruction_p1_(raw).wav

Several recordings from Dave Ibach's tape collection won't process at

all, but I'm not even sure that some of these have data in them.

They're generally quite short, but that might mean they're programs 

assembled with the General Video Assembler.  In version 2, with either

the -l1 or -l3 option, all of these fail to halt except Assembler

Unknown 1, which has a synchronization error.

Examples:

all_machine_instruction_p19_(raw).wav
assembler_unknown_1_(raw).wav
bug_puzzle_number_2_p3_(raw).wav
frog_leap_p6_(raw).wav



Section 3:  Recordings that have been processed, but demonstrate bugs

in Ballybin version 2--

Lance's recording of Alien Invasion won't process in Ballybin v2,

failing to halt with the -l3 option and giving a bad stop bit with the

may be a small glitch where it displays a question mark after loading

the title screen.

Example:

Both 2-4K Segment files from Russ's collection crash Ballybin when

using the -l1 option and make it fail to halt when using the -l3

option.  These seem to process correctly in v1.4, but I believe they

require a RAM expansion to run.  There is a very similar problem with

the 300 to 2000 baud conversion program (not sure how this works) and

the Bally Machine Load program (not sure what this is).  An extremely

short recording called joystick+stuff (not sure what this is)

error in version 1.4.  In version 1.2 it will process, but doesn't

Examples:

2-4k_segments_1_and_2_(input (24576))_side_2_(raw).wav
300-2000_baud_conversion_routine_(raw).wav
bally_machine_load_(raw).wav

icbm_attack_(v1)_(raw)_[brett_bilbrey].wav

The recordings I made from Dave Ibach's tape collection tended not to

process very well with Ballybin version 2.  I got much better results

with older versions, particularly version 1.2.  With a recording of

Avalanche, version 2 fails to halt with the -l3 option and only

partially decodes the data with the -l1 option, producing a file that

crashes when loaded.  If you use Ballybin v1.2 with the -l3 option,

you get a good output file.  Hang Up has similar problems.  In version

versions have problems with the timing between loads.  You can get a

Examples:

Often, Ballybin has difficult recognizing that some of the General

White's compilation tape makes Ballybin fail to halt in version 2, and

in the older versions, only the first load is recognized.

Example:

general_video_assembler_pass_ii_(raw).wav



Section 4:  Feature requests--

The most wanted feature is definitely 300 baud support.  We now have a

large collection of 300 baud recordings, but some won't load

correctly, and even the ones that do take up a large amount of space.

Ideally, 2000 and 300 baud support would be integrated together.  Then

we could easily convert between the formats, at least for BASIC-only

Also, Adam has suggested a raw mode.  Perhaps he could give more

Ballybin Bug Report
by Paul Thacker
April 30, 2006



Introduction

This report details some of the difficulties I've encountered when

using Ballybin and Astrowav.  I focus on the most recent iteration,

version 2 beta, but also reference version 1.4 and version 1.2 in

cases where these work better than the current version.  To ensure

consistency, I will include the versions I've used for testing, along

with .bat files I used to speed the processing.  For each version,

there is a batch-l1.bat file and a batch-l3.bat file.  Each calls

Ballybin to process every .wav file in the current directory, then

calls Astrowav to process every .bin/.bml file in the current

directory.  The only difference is that batch-l1.bat uses the -l1

option in Ballybin and batch-l3.bat uses the -l3 option.  Each file

referenced as an example is also included.

There are five major sections.  First, I discuss a problem converting

human-written .bml files to .wav files with Astrowav.  Then, I mention

a problem in decoding to BASIC discovered by Lance.  Next, I give

several examples of recordings that can't be processed with any

version of Ballybin.  It would be particularly good to get these

working, as there are no other known sources.  Next, I mention some

files that have been processed, but don't work correctly in the

current version.  These should be good for finding bugs, as the

recordings are proven to be good enough to make processing possible.

Finally, some desired additional features are mentioned.



Section 1:  BML conversion bug--

If you create a .bml file by hand and then run Astrowav v2 on it, the

resulting file can be very short and not allow the end of program

pointer to be set when loading.  In the example I created, if you run

the program, then list it, the comment on the first line is

overwritten.  See message #2536 in the Bally Alley group for more

details.  Example files:

weird_(hand_written)_[tim_hays].bml
weird_(no_end_of_program_pointer)_[tim_hays].wav

Lance mentioned having trouble decoding to BASIC with the command

"ballybin -d1 filename".  I believe there were several instances, but

I haven't tested this option very thoroughly.  On example is Frog Leap

Section 5:  Feature requests--

The most wanted feature is definitely 300 baud support.  We now have a

large collection of 300 baud recordings, but some won't load

correctly, and even the ones that do take up a large amount of space.

Ideally, 2000 and 300 baud support would be integrated together.  Then

we could easily convert between the formats, at least for BASIC-only

programs.

Also, Adam has suggested a raw mode.  Perhaps he could give more

details about what he wants and why it would be useful.

The bug report looks fine.  You didn't seem sure as to what the exact point of a RAW mode would be.  The purpose would be to spit out EXACTLY what it on the tape, spaces and all.  So, for instance, if there were a long program followed by a short burst, the current version of Ballybin doesn't like that.  That might be fixed in an update.  But is Ballybin going to be updated every time a small fix needs to be made?  Probably not.  For that reason, having a RAW mode would be an ideal solution.  Ballybin doesn't have to "process" the original file at all, it just spits out a cleaned up version of what it got.  Not only would prove useful for future programs that might not be compatible, but it may also help archive difficult programs.
